modules.title: 1 · From AR(1) to VAR (joint dynamics)
modules.summary: How stacking several AR equations into one system lets each variable depend on the lagged values of all the others.

stages.title: One series at a time: AR(1)
stages.html:
Recap: the AR(1) model

A single time series y follows an autoregression of order 1 when today's value is a constant plus a fraction of yesterday's value plus noise:

yₜ = c + φ·yₜ₋₁ + εₜ

The coefficient φ is the persistence: if φ = 0.8, a shock today still leaves 0.8 of itself tomorrow, 0.64 the day after, and so on, decaying geometrically. The series is stationary (it doesn't wander off to infinity) precisely when |φ| < 1.

The problem AR(1) ignores

Real economic variables move together. Interest rates respond to inflation; inflation responds to past output; output responds to past rates. An AR(1) on inflation alone pretends inflation only listens to its own past — it is deaf to everything else. We need a model where each variable can depend on the recent past of every variable.

Key idea. A VAR is just several AR equations estimated jointly, where the right-hand side of every equation contains the lags of every variable in the system.

stages.title: Stacking equations into a VAR(1)
stages.html:
The VAR(1) system

Take two series, y1 and y2. A VAR(1) writes one equation for each:

y1ₜ = c₁ + a₁₁·y1ₜ₋₁ + a₁₂·y2ₜ₋₁ + ε1ₜ

y2ₜ = c₂ + a₂₁·y1ₜ₋₁ + a₂₂·y2ₜ₋₁ + ε2ₜ

Collect the variables into a vector Yₜ = (y1ₜ, y2ₜ)′ and the coefficients into a 2×2 matrix A. The whole system becomes one compact line:

Yₜ = c + A·Yₜ₋₁ + εₜ

The matrix entries have crisp meanings:

  • Diagonal a₁₁, a₂₂ — each variable's own persistence (like φ in AR(1)).
  • Off-diagonal a₁₂, a₂₁ — the spillover from one variable's past into the other's present. These are exactly what a single-equation AR throws away.

When is a VAR stable?

The univariate rule |φ| < 1 generalizes: a VAR(1) is stationary when every eigenvalue of A has modulus less than 1. The eigenvalues are the multivariate analogue of φ — they govern how shocks decay through the coupled system.

Key idea. Diagonal = memory of yourself; off-diagonal = how you push the other variable around. Stability is governed by the eigenvalues of A, not the individual entries.

stages.title: Simulate and recover a VAR(1)
stages.note: We build data from a known 2×2 matrix A, then let statsmodels recover it. Compare the printed coefficients to the true A.
stages.code:
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from statsmodels.tsa.api import VAR
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

# True coefficient matrix: strong own-persistence, modest spillovers
A = np.array([[0.6, 0.2],
              [0.1, 0.5]])
print('eigenvalues |.| =', np.round(np.abs(np.linalg.eigvals(A)), 3), '(all < 1 => stable)')

n = 1000
Y = np.zeros((n, 2))
for t in range(1, n):
    Y[t] = A @ Y[t-1] + rng.normal(0, 1, 2)

df = pd.DataFrame(Y, columns=['y1', 'y2'])
res = VAR(df).fit(maxlags=1)

print('\nTrue A:\n', A)
print('\nEstimated A (res.coefs[0]):\n', np.round(res.coefs[0], 3))
print('\nFull readable summary:')
print(res.summary())

stages.title: Watch the two series co-move
stages.note: Push up the spillover a₂₁ and see how a wiggle in y1 starts dragging y2 along. Keep diagonals < 1 for stability.
stages.template:
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
A = np.array([[{{a11}}, 0.2],
              [{{a21}}, {{a22}}]])
ev = np.max(np.abs(np.linalg.eigvals(A)))
n = 300
Y = np.zeros((n, 2))
for t in range(1, n):
    Y[t] = A @ Y[t-1] + rng.normal(0, 1, 2)
plt.figure(figsize=(6,3.7))
plt.plot(Y[:,0], color='#da9100', lw=1.3, label='y1')
plt.plot(Y[:,1], color='#6f6b57', lw=1.3, label='y2')
plt.legend(loc='upper right', fontsize=8)
stab = 'STABLE' if ev < 1 else 'EXPLOSIVE'
plt.title(f'max|eigenvalue| = {ev:.2f}  ->  {stab}')

stages.title: Check: what makes it a VAR?
stages.prompt: In the VAR(1) matrix A, what does a non-zero off-diagonal entry a₁₂ represent?
choices: The persistence of y1 (how much of its own past it keeps)
The effect of last period's y2 on this period's y1
The contemporaneous correlation of the two error terms
The long-run mean of y1
stages.hint: Read off the first equation: y1ₜ = c₁ + a₁₁·y1ₜ₋₁ + a₁₂·y2ₜ₋₁ + ε1ₜ.
stages.explain: a₁₂ multiplies the lagged value of the OTHER variable (y2ₜ₋₁) in the equation for y1, so it is the cross-variable spillover; own-persistence lives on the diagonal.

stages.title: Check: stability
choices: every entry of A is less than 1 in absolute value
the determinant of A is positive
every eigenvalue of A has modulus less than 1
the off-diagonal entries are zero
stages.hint: It is the multivariate version of the AR(1) rule |φ| < 1.
stages.explain: Stationarity depends on the eigenvalues of A, not the raw entries — a matrix with large entries can still be stable, and one with small entries can be explosive.

stages.title: Does the spillover die out?
stages.prompt: A shock δ = 1 hits y1 at time 0 in a stable VAR(1) with coefficient matrix A. The horizon-2 response of the system is A²·δ. If A = [[0.5, 0.4],[0.0, 0.5]], enter the horizon-2 response of y1 (first component of A²·δ, where δ = (1, 0)′), to two decimals.
stages.hint: δ = (1,0)′, so you only need the (1,1) entry of A². For this upper-triangular A that is just 0.5².
stages.explain: The 'spillover never fades' trap. The horizon-h response is Aʰ·δ; here A²·δ has first component (0.5² + 0.4·0) = 0.25, down from 0.5 at horizon 1 and heading to 0. Because A is stable (both eigenvalues 0.5, modulus < 1), shocks are transitory and decay geometrically. Boundary: if any eigenvalue of A had modulus ≥ 1 the series would be non-stationary and the response would not die out — stability, not the size of the raw entries, is what guarantees decay.

modules.title: 2 · Estimation & lag selection
modules.summary: How a VAR is fit equation-by-equation with OLS, and how information criteria pick the lag length p.

stages.title: Estimating a VAR is just OLS, k times
stages.html:
Each equation is its own regression

A VAR(p) regresses each variable on p lags of all variables. Because every equation has the same right-hand-side regressors (the stacked lags), running OLS separately on each equation is fully efficient — there is nothing to gain from a fancier joint estimator. So fitting a k-variable VAR(p) is literally k ordinary OLS regressions.

What ties the equations together is not the estimation but the residual covariance matrix Σ. The shocks ε1ₜ and ε2ₜ are usually correlated within a period (a surprise that hits output often hits inflation the same quarter). That contemporaneous correlation lives entirely in Σ and becomes crucial later for impulse responses.

Choosing the lag length p

How many lags? Too few and you miss real dynamics (biased, autocorrelated residuals); too many and you burn degrees of freedom estimating noise (a VAR(p) on k variables has k·(k·p+1) parameters — it grows fast). We trade fit against parsimony with information criteria:

  • AIC — light penalty, tends to pick more lags; good for forecasting.
  • BIC (a.k.a. SC) — heavy penalty (∝ log n), picks fewer lags; consistent for the true order.
  • HQIC — in between.
  • FPE — final prediction error, close to AIC.
Key idea. Fit = k separate OLS regressions. Lag choice = minimize an information criterion that rewards fit and punishes the parameter count.

stages.title: select_order: read the criteria table
stages.note: We simulate a true VAR(2) and print the IC table. Each criterion reports the lag it would choose. Watch BIC pick fewer lags than AIC.
stages.code:
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from statsmodels.tsa.api import VAR
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

# True process is VAR(2): A1 then A2 act on successive lags
A1 = np.array([[0.5, 0.1],[0.0, 0.5]])
A2 = np.array([[0.0, 0.2],[0.2, 0.0]])
n = 1000
Y = np.zeros((n, 2))
for t in range(2, n):
    Y[t] = A1 @ Y[t-1] + A2 @ Y[t-2] + rng.normal(0, 1, 2)
df = pd.DataFrame(Y, columns=['y1','y2'])

sel = VAR(df).select_order(maxlags=8)
print(sel.summary())
print('\nLag chosen by each criterion:')
print(sel.selected_orders)

stages.title: Fit by an information criterion automatically
stages.note: Pass ic='aic' and statsmodels searches lags up to maxlags and keeps the best. Then we sanity-check the residuals are close to white noise.
stages.code:
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from statsmodels.tsa.api import VAR
from statsmodels.stats.stattools import durbin_watson
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
A1 = np.array([[0.5, 0.1],[0.0, 0.5]])
A2 = np.array([[0.0, 0.2],[0.2, 0.0]])
n = 1000
Y = np.zeros((n, 2))
for t in range(2, n):
    Y[t] = A1 @ Y[t-1] + A2 @ Y[t-2] + rng.normal(0, 1, 2)
df = pd.DataFrame(Y, columns=['y1','y2'])

res = VAR(df).fit(maxlags=8, ic='aic')
print('Lag order chosen by AIC:', res.k_ar)
print('Shape of coefficient array res.coefs (p, k, k):', res.coefs.shape)
print('\nResidual covariance Sigma:\n', np.round(res.sigma_u, 3))
print('\nDurbin-Watson per equation (near 2 = no leftover autocorrelation):')
print(np.round(durbin_watson(res.resid.values), 2))

stages.title: Sample size vs the lag BIC picks
stages.note: The data are truly VAR(2). With few observations, criteria get noisy; as n grows, BIC should home in on lag 2. Move the slider and read the chosen lags in the title.
stages.template:
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from statsmodels.tsa.api import VAR
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
A1 = np.array([[0.5, 0.1],[0.0, 0.5]])
A2 = np.array([[0.0, 0.2],[0.2, 0.0]])
n = int({{n}})
Y = np.zeros((n, 2))
for t in range(2, n):
    Y[t] = A1 @ Y[t-1] + A2 @ Y[t-2] + rng.normal(0, 1, 2)
df = pd.DataFrame(Y, columns=['y1','y2'])
maxlags = 8
sel = VAR(df).select_order(maxlags=maxlags)
aics, bics = [], []
base = VAR(df)
for p in range(1, maxlags+1):
    r = base.fit(p)
    aics.append(r.aic); bics.append(r.bic)
lags = np.arange(1, maxlags+1)
plt.figure(figsize=(6,3.7))
plt.plot(lags, aics, 'o-', color='#da9100', label='AIC')
plt.plot(lags, bics, 's-', color='#6f6b57', label='BIC')
plt.axvline(2, color='#c9c6ac', ls='--', lw=1)
plt.xlabel('lag p'); plt.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.title(f"n={n}: AIC picks {sel.selected_orders['aic']}, BIC picks {sel.selected_orders['bic']} (truth=2)")

stages.title: Check: which criterion?
stages.prompt: You care most about not overfitting and want the most parsimonious lag order that is consistent for the true p. Which criterion do you lean on?
choices: AIC
BIC (SC)
FPE
always use the maximum lag
stages.hint: One of these has a penalty that grows with log(n) and is the strictest.
stages.explain: BIC's penalty (∝ log n · #params) is the harshest, so it selects fewer lags and is consistent for the true order; AIC/FPE favor richer models better suited to pure forecasting.

stages.title: Check: estimation method
stages.prompt: Why can a VAR be estimated by running OLS separately on each equation without losing efficiency?
choices: Because the errors are independent across equations
Because every equation shares exactly the same set of regressors (the stacked lags)
Because OLS is always efficient
Because the residual covariance Σ is diagonal
stages.hint: Think about what SUR/GLS would buy you when all equations have identical regressors.
stages.explain: When every equation has the same regressors, the GLS (SUR) estimator collapses to equation-by-equation OLS, so separate OLS is already fully efficient even though the errors are correlated across equations.

stages.title: Which criterion picks the fewest lags?
stages.prompt: Among AIC, BIC, and HQIC, the criterion with the harshest penalty (∝ log n · #params) — so it selects the fewest lags and is consistent for the true order — is ___.
stages.lead: select_order printed AIC, BIC, and HQIC side by side; you must name the one that penalizes extra parameters hardest.
stages.hint: Its penalty grows with log n, so it punishes extra parameters harder than AIC as the sample grows.
stages.explain: The all-criteria-agree assumption. BIC (a.k.a. SC / Schwarz) carries the heaviest penalty (∝ log n per parameter), so it selects fewer lags and is consistent for the true lag order. AIC and FPE use a lighter, fixed penalty and tend to pick more lags — better for pure forecasting, not for recovering the true order. Boundary: when the goal is forecasting rather than identifying the true p, the richer AIC model can legitimately win, so the criteria need not, and often do not, agree.

modules.title: 3 · Impulse-response functions & FEVD
modules.summary: Tracing how a one-time shock to one variable ripples through the system over time, and how to split forecast uncertainty across shocks.

stages.title: What an impulse response answers
stages.html:
Impulse-response functions (IRFs)

The coefficient matrix A is hard to read directly. The impulse-response function turns it into a story: if variable j gets a one-time, one-unit shock today and nothing else happens, what is the path of every variable over the next h periods?

Mechanically, the response at horizon h is just powers of A acting on the shock. For a VAR(1) a shock δ hitting at time 0 produces responses δ, A·δ, A²·δ, A³·δ, … — the system's memory unrolling. Because A is stable, these fade to zero: shocks are transitory.

Why orthogonalize?

There's a catch. The raw shocks ε1 and ε2 are correlated (that's Σ from Module 2). A 'shock to y1 alone' is then ill-defined — in the data, y1 surprises and y2 surprises arrive together. To get clean, isolated shocks we orthogonalize using a Cholesky factor of Σ. This imposes an ordering: the first variable can affect the second contemporaneously, but not vice-versa within the same period.

Key idea. orth_irfs gives uncorrelated structural shocks via the Cholesky factor of Σ, but the answer depends on variable ordering. Reorder the columns and the impact responses can change.

stages.title: Plot the four orthogonalized IRFs
stages.note: We simulate CORRELATED shocks (corr 0.6) so Σ is non-diagonal and orthogonalization actually does something. orth_irfs is indexed [horizon, response variable, shock variable]; we draw all 4 paths and print the impact matrix.
stages.code:
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from statsmodels.tsa.api import VAR
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
A = np.array([[0.6, 0.2],[0.1, 0.5]])
# Correlated structural shocks: L is a Cholesky factor of a 0.6-correlation matrix
L = np.linalg.cholesky(np.array([[1.0, 0.6],[0.6, 1.0]]))
n = 1000
Y = np.zeros((n, 2))
for t in range(1, n):
    Y[t] = A @ Y[t-1] + L @ rng.normal(0, 1, 2)
df = pd.DataFrame(Y, columns=['y1','y2'])
res = VAR(df).fit(maxlags=1)
print('Residual covariance Sigma (note the non-zero off-diagonal):\n', np.round(res.sigma_u, 3))

H = 12
irf = res.irf(H)
o = irf.orth_irfs   # shape (H+1, 2, 2): [horizon, response, shock]
h = np.arange(H+1)
names = ['y1','y2']
fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(6, 4.4), sharex=True)
for sh in range(2):      # which variable is shocked
    for rp in range(2):  # which variable responds
        a = ax[rp, sh]
        a.axhline(0, color='#c9c6ac', lw=.8)
        a.plot(h, o[:, rp, sh], color='#da9100', lw=1.8)
        a.set_title(f'{names[sh]} shock -> {names[rp]}', fontsize=8)
for a in ax[1]:
    a.set_xlabel('horizon')
fig.tight_layout()
print('\nImpact (h=0) matrix [response x shock]:\n', np.round(o[0], 3))

stages.title: FEVD: who drives forecast uncertainty?
stages.note: With correlated shocks the cross-shares are meaningful. The forecast-error variance decomposition splits each variable's h-step forecast variance into shares per shock; shares sum to 1 across each row.
stages.code:
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from statsmodels.tsa.api import VAR
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
A = np.array([[0.6, 0.2],[0.1, 0.5]])
L = np.linalg.cholesky(np.array([[1.0, 0.6],[0.6, 1.0]]))
n = 1000
Y = np.zeros((n, 2))
for t in range(1, n):
    Y[t] = A @ Y[t-1] + L @ rng.normal(0, 1, 2)
df = pd.DataFrame(Y, columns=['y1','y2'])
res = VAR(df).fit(maxlags=1)

fevd = res.fevd(10)
print(fevd.summary())
# decomp[i] is the (horizons x k) table for variable i: cols = shock shares
share_y1_from_y2 = fevd.decomp[0][-1, 1]
print(f'\nAt horizon 10, share of y1 forecast variance due to the y2 shock: {share_y1_from_y2:.3f}')

stages.title: Slide persistence & spillover, redraw the IRF
stages.note: Shocks are correlated (corr 0.6). This redraws the response of BOTH variables to a single orthogonalized shock in y1. More persistence (a₁₁) => slower decay; more spillover (a₂₁) => bigger hump in y2's response.
stages.template:
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from statsmodels.tsa.api import VAR
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
A = np.array([[{{a11}}, 0.2],[{{a21}}, 0.5]])
L = np.linalg.cholesky(np.array([[1.0, 0.6],[0.6, 1.0]]))
n = 600
Y = np.zeros((n, 2))
for t in range(1, n):
    Y[t] = A @ Y[t-1] + L @ rng.normal(0, 1, 2)
df = pd.DataFrame(Y, columns=['y1','y2'])
res = VAR(df).fit(maxlags=1)
H = 12
o = res.irf(H).orth_irfs   # [horizon, response, shock]
h = np.arange(H+1)
peak_y2 = np.max(np.abs(o[:, 1, 0]))
plt.figure(figsize=(6,3.7))
plt.axhline(0, color='#c9c6ac', lw=.8)
plt.plot(h, o[:, 0, 0], color='#da9100', lw=2, label='y1 response')
plt.plot(h, o[:, 1, 0], color='#6f6b57', lw=2, label='y2 response')
plt.legend(fontsize=8); plt.xlabel('horizon')
plt.title(f'Response to a y1 shock | peak |y2 response| = {peak_y2:.2f}')

stages.title: Check: ordering matters
stages.prompt: You compute orthogonalized IRFs, then swap the order of the two columns in your DataFrame and recompute. What can change?
choices: Nothing — orthogonalization is order-invariant
The contemporaneous (impact) responses, because the Cholesky ordering changes which variable can affect the other within the same period
Only the long-run responses
The estimated coefficient matrix A
stages.hint: Cholesky imposes a recursive timing assumption based on column order.
stages.explain: Orthogonalization via Cholesky assumes earlier-ordered variables can hit later ones contemporaneously but not the reverse; changing the order changes that assumption and hence the impact responses.

stages.title: Check: reading FEVD
stages.prompt: A FEVD says that at horizon 10, 85% of y1's forecast-error variance comes from its own shock and 15% from the y2 shock. This means…
choices: y1 is mostly driven by its own innovations at that horizon
y2 Granger-causes y1 with p < 0.15
the IRF of y1 to a y2 shock is exactly 0.15
y1 and y2 are uncorrelated
stages.hint: FEVD shares are about variance attribution, and they sum to 1 across shocks for each variable.
stages.explain: FEVD splits a variable's forecast uncertainty into shares per shock; 85% own-share means y1's unpredictability is mostly self-generated at horizon 10, with y2 contributing only 15%.

stages.title: Significant VAR coefficient: what does it prove?
stages.prompt: In your fitted reduced-form VAR, the lagged-X coefficient in the Y equation is large and highly significant, and the orthogonalized IRF of Y to an X shock is clearly non-zero. The safest reading is:
choices: X structurally causes Y — the significant coefficient settles it
Past X carries predictive information about Y; calling it a structural effect needs an imposed identification (the ordering)
Reordering the Cholesky variables would leave the impact responses unchanged
The IRF is structural automatically because it came from orth_irfs
why: Significance is reduced-form predictive content, not proof of a structural mechanism.
Reordering changes which variable can hit the other contemporaneously, so impact responses do change.
orth_irfs imposes an ordering you chose; that choice IS the identifying assumption, it is not automatic.
stages.hint: A reduced-form VAR is silent about structure until you impose an assumption.
stages.explain: The reduced-form-significance-is-structural trap. A significant lag coefficient (or a non-zero orthogonalized IRF) is predictive precedence — exactly Granger content — not a verified structural effect. The orthogonalized IRF only looks structural because you supplied a Cholesky ordering; reorder the variables and the impact responses move. Boundary: the structural reading is valid only when the ordering's contemporaneous-causal assumption is itself defensible, which the data cannot confirm.

stages.title: Are IRFs structural for free?
stages.prompt: Claim: you can read structural impulse responses straight off a reduced-form VAR with no identifying assumption — orth_irfs just returns them.
stages.hint: What did you have to choose before the Cholesky factor was even defined?
stages.explain: The IRFs-are-structural-for-free trap. Orthogonalized IRFs require a Cholesky factor of Σ, and that factor depends on a variable ordering you impose: the earlier variable may hit the later one contemporaneously but not vice versa. Reorder the columns and the impact responses change — so the structure came from your assumption, not the data. Boundary: the reduced-form VAR alone pins down forecasts and correlations; turning those into structural shocks always needs an extra identifying restriction (ordering, sign restrictions, or external instruments).

modules.title: 4 · Granger causality & forecasting
modules.summary: Testing whether one variable's past helps predict another, and producing and reading multi-step VAR forecasts.

stages.title: Granger causality: prediction, not philosophy
stages.html:
Does y2's past help predict y1?

Granger causality has a deliberately modest definition: y2 Granger-causes y1 if the past of y2 contains information that improves the forecast of y1, beyond what y1's own past already provides. It is a statement about predictive content, not about true cause and effect — y2 could merely be a leading indicator.

In a VAR this becomes a clean joint test. y2 fails to Granger-cause y1 exactly when all the coefficients on lagged y2 in the y1 equation are zero:

H₀: a₁₂⁽¹⁾ = a₁₂⁽²⁾ = … = a₁₂⁽ᵖ⁾ = 0

That's an F-test (or Wald χ²) on a block of coefficients. A small p-value rejects H₀ → y2 does carry predictive information about y1.

Key idea. Granger causality = 'past of X improves the forecast of Y'. It is a block-of-zeros F-test on the off-diagonal lag coefficients, and it is about prediction, not deep causation.

stages.title: Run the causality test both directions
stages.note: We build data where y1's past genuinely drives y2 but NOT the reverse. The test should reject in one direction and not the other.
stages.code:
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from statsmodels.tsa.api import VAR
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

# y2 listens to y1 (a21=0.4), but y1 ignores y2 (a12=0)
A = np.array([[0.5, 0.0],
              [0.4, 0.5]])
n = 1000
Y = np.zeros((n, 2))
for t in range(1, n):
    Y[t] = A @ Y[t-1] + rng.normal(0, 1, 2)
df = pd.DataFrame(Y, columns=['y1','y2'])
res = VAR(df).fit(maxlags=1)

t1 = res.test_causality('y2', ['y1'], kind='f')  # does y1 help predict y2?
t2 = res.test_causality('y1', ['y2'], kind='f')  # does y2 help predict y1?
print('y1 -> y2 :  p =', round(t1.pvalue, 4), '=>', 'REJECT H0 (y1 helps)' if t1.pvalue < 0.05 else 'cannot reject')
print('y2 -> y1 :  p =', round(t2.pvalue, 4), '=>', 'REJECT H0 (y2 helps)' if t2.pvalue < 0.05 else 'cannot reject')

stages.title: Spillover strength vs the Granger p-value
stages.note: Crank a₂₁ (how much y1's past feeds into y2). As the true spillover grows, the test for 'y1 → y2' should reject ever more decisively (tiny p-value).
stages.template:
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from statsmodels.tsa.api import VAR
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
A = np.array([[0.5, 0.0],[{{a21}}, 0.5]])
n = 500
Y = np.zeros((n, 2))
for t in range(1, n):
    Y[t] = A @ Y[t-1] + rng.normal(0, 1, 2)
df = pd.DataFrame(Y, columns=['y1','y2'])
res = VAR(df).fit(maxlags=1)
p = res.test_causality('y2', ['y1'], kind='f').pvalue
plt.figure(figsize=(6,3.7))
plt.plot(Y[:150,0], color='#da9100', lw=1.2, label='y1')
plt.plot(Y[:150,1], color='#6f6b57', lw=1.2, label='y2')
plt.legend(fontsize=8, loc='upper right')
verdict = 'REJECT H0' if p < 0.05 else 'cannot reject'
plt.title(f'Granger y1->y2:  p = {p:.4f}  ({verdict})')

stages.title: Forecast h steps ahead with bands
stages.note: forecast_interval() needs the last p observations as a seed and returns the point forecast plus lower/upper bands. We plot history, the point forecast, and an approximate 95% interval.
stages.code:
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from statsmodels.tsa.api import VAR
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
A = np.array([[0.6, 0.2],[0.1, 0.5]])
n = 400
Y = np.zeros((n, 2))
for t in range(1, n):
    Y[t] = A @ Y[t-1] + rng.normal(0, 1, 2)
df = pd.DataFrame(Y, columns=['y1','y2'])
res = VAR(df).fit(maxlags=1)
lags = res.k_ar

steps = 15
# point forecast + analytic forecast-error interval
mid, lower, upper = res.forecast_interval(df.values[-lags:], steps, alpha=0.05)
print('First 3 forecast rows [y1, y2]:\n', np.round(mid[:3], 3))

fut = np.arange(n, n+steps)
plt.figure(figsize=(6,3.7))
plt.plot(np.arange(n-40, n), Y[-40:,0], color='#6f6b57', lw=1.2, label='y1 history')
plt.plot(fut, mid[:,0], color='#da9100', lw=2, label='y1 forecast')
plt.fill_between(fut, lower[:,0], upper[:,0], color='#af983f', alpha=.3, label='95% band')
plt.axvline(n, color='#c9c6ac', ls='--', lw=1)
plt.legend(fontsize=8); plt.title('VAR forecast of y1 with 95% interval')

stages.title: Check: what Granger causality is (and isn't)
stages.prompt: A test finds that y2 Granger-causes y1 (p = 0.001). The safest interpretation is:
choices: Changing y2 will mechanically change y1 — true causation is proven
Past values of y2 improve forecasts of y1 beyond y1's own past
y1 and y2 must be contemporaneously uncorrelated
y1 cannot also Granger-cause y2
stages.hint: The name is misleading; it is fundamentally a statement about forecasting.
stages.explain: Granger causality only certifies predictive content of y2's history for y1; it does not establish structural causation, allows correlation, and is not exclusive (causality can run both ways).

stages.title: Check: forecast bands
stages.prompt: As the forecast horizon h grows, the width of a VAR's forecast interval typically…
choices: shrinks toward zero
stays constant
widens and then levels off at the stationary (unconditional) variance
oscillates without bound
stages.hint: For a stable VAR, the forecast converges to the mean and the forecast-error variance converges to a finite limit.
stages.explain: Forecast-error variance accumulates with horizon but, because the VAR is stationary, it converges to the series' unconditional variance, so the bands widen and then flatten rather than growing forever.

stages.title: Does Granger causality mean causation?
stages.prompt: You just ran the block F-test and found that X Granger-causes Y (p = 0.001). Claim: this proves that X causes Y — intervening on X would move Y.
stages.hint: Read the name literally as a forecasting statement, not a philosophical one.
stages.explain: The Granger-is-causation trap. Granger causality only says past X improves the forecast of Y beyond Y's own past — it is predictive precedence, not structural cause. A common driver or anticipation (X is a leading indicator) yields Granger causality with no causal link from X to Y. Boundary: a structural causal claim needs an identifying assumption you impose (e.g. a Cholesky ordering); no in-sample F-test can supply it.

stages.title: What's true about a reduced-form VAR?
stages.prompt: Select all that apply. Which statements about a reduced-form VAR are TRUE?
choices: Granger causality means predictive precedence, not structural causation
Cholesky-orthogonalized impulse responses depend on the variable ordering you impose
Estimating in non-stationary levels can read spurious dynamics as real
A statistically significant lag coefficient proves X structurally causes Y
Adding more lags is always the safer choice
stages.hint: Two of these are the headline VAR traps — a significant coefficient is predictive, and more lags is not free.
stages.explain: Two traps are bundled here. TRUE: Granger = predictive precedence; orthogonalized IRFs hinge on the ordering you impose; a level VAR on unit-root series can manufacture spurious dynamics (difference or use a VECM if cointegrated). FALSE: a significant coefficient is reduced-form prediction, never structural proof — the structural-from-significance trap; and 'more lags is always safer' burns degrees of freedom (a k-variable VAR(p) has k·(k·p+1) parameters) and overfits. Boundary: more lags only helps when residual autocorrelation says you genuinely under-fit; otherwise an information criterion like BIC trims it back.
